subject: Culture
title: Moving Out
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Moving Out.

hook.text: In the US, living with parents past 25 carries stigma. In Italy, it's normal well into your 30s.

buildup.text: Anglo-Saxon culture treats leaving home as proof of independence. Adulthood requires a separate address.

discovery.text: In many Asian and Latin cultures, children stay until marriage—or even after. Multigenerational homes are the norm.

twist.text: Rising housing costs are forcing Western millennials back home. Economic reality is rewriting the cultural script.

climax.text: Whether leaving home is triumph or tragedy depends entirely on the culture measuring it.

punchline.text: Independence looks different in every zip code.

quiz.question: In which cultural context is living with parents into your 30s considered normal?

details.summary: Leaving the family home is a major rite of passage whose timing varies dramatically by culture. Americans leave around 18, Scandinavians even earlier, while Mediterranean and Asian cultures keep children at home into their 30s. What feels natural in one culture seems bizarre in another.
details.whyItMatters: The age of leaving home reflects deep cultural values about independence, family obligation, and adulthood. It directly shapes housing markets, economic structures, and family relationships.
takeaways: Americans typically leave home around 18 for college or work
In Italy, the average age of leaving home is around 30
Multigenerational living is the global norm, not the exception

faq.question: Why do Americans leave home so young?
faq.answer: American culture strongly values individual independence and self-reliance. The college system physically separates 18-year-olds from family. Staying home past early twenties often carries stigma.

faq.question: Why do Mediterranean cultures keep children at home longer?
faq.answer: In Italy, Spain, and Greece, family-centered values prioritize staying together. Economic factors also play a role — youth unemployment, expensive housing, and lower starting salaries make independence harder to achieve. Culturally, there is no stigma in living with parents.
